questions.q: Per this lesson, what makes a decision a genuine "tradeoff" rather than simply a right-or-wrong choice?
options: Gaining more of one desirable quality costs you some of another desirable quality, so no option maximizes everything
One option is objectively better on every dimension that matters
The decision was made quickly, without much analysis
The organization lacks the budget to implement either option
questions.explain: If one option were simply better across every quality that matters, there would be nothing to trade off -- it would just be the right answer. A real tradeoff always costs you something on one axis to gain something on another.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against treating 'best practice' as a universal rule?
options: Best practices are always outdated and should never be followed
A best practice is usually a previously-made tradeoff that was correct for a specific context, repeated without that context attached
Best practices only apply to Apex code, never to declarative tools
Salesforce does not publish any best-practice guidance
questions.explain: Most 'best practices' are tradeoff decisions someone already made for a specific organization's constraints -- the advice survived, but the context that made it correct often got dropped along the way.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what distinguishes a well-made tradeoff from an architecture mistake?
options: A well-made tradeoff has no downside at all
A mistake is any decision that costs money

A mistake is choosing without understanding the cost, or applying a different org's answer to your own context; a well-made tradeoff is a known cost, confirmed as acceptable, with the reasoning documented
There is no real difference -- every tradeoff is technically a mistake
questions.explain: You're not accountable for finding an option with zero downside -- none exists. You're accountable for knowing the downside, confirming the organization can live with it, and being able to explain that reasoning later.

questions.q: What is the third of the three questions this lesson says every tradeoff decision should answer?
options: What are we optimizing for, and what are we willing to spend to get it?
What does this specific organization actually need right now and going forward?
Which vendor offers the lowest licensing cost for this feature?
What happens when the context changes, and under what conditions should this decision be revisited?
questions.explain: The third question asks what happens if the organization's scale, regulatory environment, or team changes -- a tradeoff correct today can become wrong later, so naming the conditions for revisiting it is part of making the decision well.

questions.q: Why might the same tradeoff (for example, synchronous vs. asynchronous integration) resolve differently for a 50-person startup than for a large regulated bank?
options: Because the two organizations have different constraints -- scale, regulatory requirements, budget, and team composition -- so the same decision can be correct for one and wrong for the other
Because Salesforce enforces different governor limits based on company size
Because startups are not permitted to use asynchronous processing
Tradeoffs always resolve the same way regardless of organization, so this wouldn't actually happen
questions.explain: Context is central to this lesson's framing: the right side of a tradeoff depends on the specific organization's needs, not on a universal rule, which is exactly why 'it depends' is often the honest and correct answer.
